Surely the most important condition, cause, consequence, and effect of placing limits on land warfare was the restriction of the concept of the enemy.
An economic competitor is not an enemy even during war.
In naval warfare, by contrast, he is an enemy. And that means that even between two wars—in other words, during peace—he remains a potential enemy.
The condition of peace between two land wars is therefore something fundamentally different from the condition of peace between two naval wars.

What “line” lies behind the atomic bomb and the other bacteriological, biological, genocidal, and similar highly scientific, highly progressive, highly modern means of fighting a “just war” in the modern sense?
Not a Maginot Line, which still had something almost touchingly terrestrial about it.
Not a global line in the sense of the Raya, the Amity Line, or the line of the Western Hemisphere. Those still imagined the globe in terms of its surface.
Instead, a space. And before that space can be filled with the proper content—cuius economia, eius regio—it must first be emptied completely and turned into a tabula rasa.
Only the elite matter. So always keep yourself close to whatever happens to be the elite.
Today’s elite are not yesterday’s elite, still less tomorrow’s or the day after tomorrow’s.
The elite are those who, while receiving the highest incomes, pay the lowest taxes.
The elite are those who can require other people to fill in questionnaires. The elite are those who can demand full and generous compensation for their own sacrifice.
The elite are those who do not have to go to the courts to obtain their rights, and who do not have to fear the courts because of their wrongs.
The elite are those who, if they have passports, do not have to collect them from the police.
The elite are those whose sociology nobody dares to write. The elite are those who can accuse others without having to fear being accused themselves.
The elite are those who are allowed to reject the tu quoque: “You did it too.”

“Suicide by the executioner’s hand” has many different levels and phases of meaning:

The outward, banal meaning: a cheap death, practically free, administered without any special expense for a doctor or funeral. Though even that is not always true, because the heirs can be held liable. But today the property is usually confiscated anyway.
A sublime Stoic experiment: treating the executioner as the freely accepted means of one’s own suicide.
The Christian meaning: receiving the executioner as a welcome messenger, like an illness or any other cause of death.

Human weapons—swords and guns—surpass the weapons of animals—horns, teeth, and stings. And by exactly the same measure, man surpasses wolves, bears, and snakes in greed and cruelty. Those animals are not ravenous beyond their hunger and do not become savage unless provoked; man can be hungry even for a hunger that is still to come.

One part of this statement expresses a very exact relationship: human beings are more cruel than predatory animals by precisely the same degree that human weapons are more powerful than the weapons of animals. That applies to swords. It applies far more strongly to modern weapons of annihilation.
Think for a moment about what that means.
I will be careful not to say any more.
The fate of the lawyer and of the legal profession on the European continent:
Since the French Revolution, from 1789 to 1848, law has split into legality and legitimacy.
[It] ends with the lawyer sinking down into mere legality. That was “positivism.”
Since 1848, this division has been followed by a division within legitimacy itself.

At first, during the Restoration from 1815 to 1830, legitimacy appeared as purely historical, dynastic, and restorative legitimacy. Then a new revolutionary legitimacy arose against it and finally won.
The test is this: having a clear conscience about legality and illegality.
The great manifesto of this victory is Lenin’s work on legality and illegality as nothing more than different methods—Left-Wing Communism: An Infantile Disorder.
Its authentic philosophy of law rests on a philosophy of history: Georg Lukács, History and Class Consciousness, 1923.

Now there is only revolutionary legitimacy. This legitimacy is capable of justifying any cruelty. It can give every imperialism the character of an act of liberation. It can give every inhuman act the character of a measure taken in the service of a higher humanity. And for everything—for wars and civil wars, for the liquidation of entire classes and peoples—it can guarantee the absolution of the World Spirit.
Today this legitimacy has been monopolized in the East.
The West has not even noticed the split between legality and legitimacy.
The Anglo-Saxons and the Catholic Church <…> still do not make this distinction. <…>
